title: Chern non-trivial two-dimensional square-net nodal line semimetal
authors: Kendall Ramos, Salvador Barraza-Lopez, Elias Andrade
abstract: We investigate a two-dimensional $p_xp_y$ square-net tight-binding model with two sublattices and introduce a symmetry-informed, momentum-dependent spin-orbit coupling (SOC) with a finite-range real-space hopping representation. Its two components jointly gap the nodal line, while one breaks time-reversal symmetry, producing a Chern-insulating phase with an occupied band Chern number $C=2$. Nanoribbon calculations reveal edge-localized states traversing this gap, with two net chiral modes per edge. We further show that the conserved spin sectors are unitarily equivalent and therefore have equal Chern numbers, ruling out a nontrivial time-reversal-protected $\mathbb{Z}_2$ phase within this ansatz. Our results establish a phenomenological route to Chern topology in square-net two-dimensional systems and clarify the symmetry constraints governing the accessible insulating phases.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to engineer Chern topology in 2D square-net semimetals using a modified tight-binding model. By introducing a momentum-dependent spin-orbit coupling that breaks time-reversal symmetry, the authors successfully opened a bulk gap and calculated a non-zero Chern number (C=2). This work establishes a general, phenomenological method for realizing such topological phases in these lattice systems.
main_problem: To establish a phenomenological route to realizing Chern topology in two-dimensional square-net systems by engineering a gap-opening coupling.
main_result: The authors successfully engineered a gap-opening coupling that results in a Chern-insulating phase with an occupied band Chern number of C=2, accompanied by edge-localized chiral edge states.
method: The analysis involves modifying a tight-binding Hamiltonian with a momentum-dependent spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and calculating the Chern number using lattice-gauge-invariant methods.
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional p_x p_y square-net tight-binding model with two sublattices. The Hamiltonian is modified by introducing a momentum-dependent term, $\eta(\mathbf{k})$, which breaks time-reversal symmetry.
key_observables: Chern number (C=2), edge-localized states with two net chiral modes per edge, and the opening of a bulk gap.
important_parameters:
The parameters $\mu$ and $\lambda$ control the gap opening; the gap opens only when both $\mu 
eq 0$ and $\lambda 
eq 0$.
main_assumptions: The construction provides a phenomenological framework, meaning it does not require a specific microscopic realization in materials like ZrSiS to achieve the topology.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the lattice structure and nodal line. Figure 2 demonstrates the gap opening in the band structure when both $\mu$ and $\lambda$ are non-zero. Figure 4 confirms the existence of edge-localized branches in nanoribbons.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the model and the need to open a gap across the nodal line. It then details the modification of the SOC term using $\eta(\mathbf{k})$ to break time-reversal symmetry. Finally, it calculates the resulting Chern number and analyzes the edge states via nanoribbon calculations.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, tunable theoretical mechanism (via engineered SOC) to realize non-trivial Chern insulators in a geometrically simple lattice structure, which is relevant for understanding topological phases in engineered quantum materials.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Square lattice with two atoms per unit-cell, the sublattices are labeled as A and B and indicated by or- ange (light) and blue (dark) circles, respectively. Each of the atoms contributes to the tight-binding Hamiltonian with px and py orbitals, shown as well. (b) First Brillouin zone of the two-atom square lattice. The black circles indicate the high-symmetry points. The spectrum features a nodal line indicated schematically by the (red) curve. The path-shown is used to plot the dispersion in (c); squares show the points where the path crosses the nodal line.

Figure 2. Band structures with the introduction of PSOC with η(k) as defined in Eq. (13) for different values of µ and λ. (a) µ = λ = 0. (b) µ = 30 meV and λ = 0. (c) µ = 0 and λ = 30 meV. (d) µ = λ = 30 meV, this is the only case where a gap is opened, as highlighted by the shaded region.

Figure 3. Mapping of the SOC η(k) in real space. (a) Inter- lattice interaction at first nearest neighbors, the magnitude of the interaction λ changes sign while moving along the x- direction. (b)-(c) Intralattice interaction for second nearest- neighbors with a imaginary amplitude µ. The signs are op- posite between sublattices. In each process there is a flip in the orbital and spin as indicated in the top-right inset.

Figure 4. Band structure for nanoribbons of width 100a. (a) µ = 0 and λ = 0, (b) µ = 30 meV and λ = 0, (c) µ = 0 and λ = 30 meV and (d) µ = 30 meV and λ = 30 meV. The bands are colored according to their localization in the transverse direction of the ribbon, such that T and B stand for top and bottom edge, respectively. Shading in (d) indicates the bulk gap.
